title: BIP-44 multi-account hierarchy
plain:
Modern Bitcoin wallets share a common filing system called BIP-44. A 'BIP' (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal) is a set of written rules that wallet makers follow so their products work the same way.

Everything starts with your seed — the short list of secret backup words a wallet gives you at setup. From that one seed, the wallet mathematically builds a huge tree of addresses. An address is the long string of letters and numbers you share to receive money. Because every address grows from the seed, one backup covers everything.

BIP-44 gives the tree five levels, like folders inside folders. A spot in the tree is written like this: m / 44' / 0' / 0' / 0 / 0.

The first level, 'purpose', is fixed at 44 and marks this part of the tree as following the BIP-44 rules. The second, 'coin type', keeps different currencies apart: Bitcoin is number 0, and Bitcoin Testnet — a practice copy of the network used for testing — is number 1. A registry called SLIP-0044 lists numbers for other currencies.

The third level, 'account', works like accounts at a bank: one for savings, one for spending, one for donations. Money never mixes between them. Wallets should refuse to create a new account if the previous one has never been used.

The fourth level is 'change': 0 marks the normal receiving addresses you show to other people; 1 marks hidden change addresses, where a wallet quietly returns your leftover money after you spend. The fifth level is simply the address number, counting up from 0. The apostrophes (as in 44') mark an extra-protected step in the math.

Two facts matter if a wallet is ever restored from its seed, as inheritors must do. The wallet finds accounts by past activity, not balances — an old, now-empty account still counts. And it stops scanning for addresses after 20 unused receiving addresses in a row (the 'gap limit'). So don't press 'new address' again and again without using them: money sent to a far-out address might not show up after a restore.
technical:
BIP-0044 defines a five-level BIP32 derivation path, m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index, as a particular application of the BIP-0043 purpose scheme. Purpose is the constant 44' (0x8000002C). Hardened derivation is used at purpose, coin_type, and account; public derivation at change and address_index.

Coin type creates a separate subtree per currency, avoiding address reuse across currencies and improving privacy. Registered types include 0' (0x80000000) Bitcoin and 1' (0x80000001) Bitcoin Testnet; SatoshiLabs maintains the full registry (SLIP-0044, https://github.com/satoshilabs/slips/blob/master/slip-0044.md). Registering a new type requires an existing wallet implementing the standard and a pull request to that file.

Accounts partition the key space into independent user identities (e.g., donations, savings, common expenses), numbered from index 0; software should prevent creating an account if the previous one has no transaction history.

Change uses constant 0 for the external chain (addresses intended to be visible outside the wallet, e.g., for receiving) and 1 for the internal chain (change addresses not intended to be visible). Address indices count up from 0.

Account discovery on seed import: derive account index 0, derive its external chain, scan addresses respecting the gap limit; if no transactions are found, stop, otherwise increment the account index and repeat. Discovery uses transaction history, not balances — a zero-balance account with prior activity still continues discovery.

The address gap limit is 20: after 20 consecutive unused addresses on an external chain, the wallet expects no used addresses beyond that point and stops searching. Only external chains are scanned, because internal chains receive only coins originating from their associated external chains. Wallets should warn when a user tries to exceed the gap limit by generating a new address.

Example: the first account's first Bitcoin address is m/44'/0'/0'/0/0.

claims.claim: One master seed can be used for an unlimited number of independent cryptocoins, and the hierarchy handles multiple coins, multiple accounts, external and internal chains per account, and millions of addresses per chain.
Separate coin-type subtrees avoid reusing addresses across cryptocoins and improve privacy.

Registered coin types include 0' (0x80000000) for Bitcoin and 1' (0x80000001) for Bitcoin Testnet; the full registry is maintained by SatoshiLabs as SLIP-0044, and registering a new coin type requires an existing wallet implementing the standard plus a pull request to that file.
claims.source: Registered coin types section and table

claims.claim: Accounts split the key space into independent user identities (e.g., donation, saving, common expenses), are numbered from index 0, and software should prevent creating an account if the previous account has no transaction history.
Constant 0 designates the external chain (addresses intended to be visible outside the wallet, e.g., for receiving payments) and constant 1 designates the internal chain (change addresses).

Account discovery after importing a seed derives each account's external chain and scans it respecting the gap limit, stopping when no transactions are found; discovery is based on transaction history, not balances, so a zero-balance account with prior activity still continues discovery.

The address gap limit is 20: if software hits 20 unused addresses in a row, it expects no used addresses beyond that point and stops searching the chain; only external chains are scanned because internal chains receive only coins from their associated external chains.
Wallet software should warn when the user tries to exceed the gap limit on an external chain by generating a new address.
The first address of the first Bitcoin account is at path m/44'/0'/0'/0/0, and the second account's first change address is at m/44'/0'/1'/1/0.
BIP-0044 was assigned 2014-04-24 and its listed status in this copy is Deployed.

warnings: Do not generate many receiving addresses without using them: after 20 unused addresses in a row (the 'gap limit'), a restored wallet stops scanning and may not display funds sent to later addresses.
Never share seed words: anyone who holds them controls every account and address that seed can create.
source_title: BIP-0044: Multi-Account Hierarchy for Deterministic Wallets
notes_for_reviewer: Several items to verify: (1) The cached copy says Status: Deployed, but the canonical bitcoin/bips page may list BIP-44 as Proposed — confirm at the source URL before publication. (2) The plain text describes the seed as a word list; that mapping is BIP-39, which this source only implies via 'master node (seed)' — consider a BIP-39 companion entry. (3) The BIP says the gap limit is 'currently set to 20' — reconfirm the value is still 20 across major wallets. (4) The consequence that funds beyond the gap limit may be missed on restore is inferred from the stop-scanning rule and the BIP's warning requirement, not stated verbatim. (5) This BIP covers the legacy purpose-44' scheme; modern wallets commonly use purpose 49'/84' paths (BIP-49/BIP-84), which is NOT in this source and was excluded from claims, but users restoring a wallet may see m/84' paths and wonder — companion entries recommended. (6) Only Bitcoin (0) and Testnet (1) coin types appear in the BIP itself; SLIP-0044 changes frequently, so the entry deliberately cites no further coin numbers to avoid staleness. (7) The claim about seed words in warnings is app-level standard guidance, not from this source.
